verified_entries.title: Debate Helps Weak Judges Reward Stronger Models
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Proposer-critic debate in a stronger-debater/weaker-judge setting on programmatically verifiable code and logic tasks helps the judge over a consultancy baseline only when the critic's classification ability exceeds the judge's and the judge treats critic speeches as claims to verify rather than testimony to summarize; on non-responder pairings debate is null and judge verification rates drop once a critic enters the transcript; ablating rebuttal rounds produces no measurable change, so a single independent critique recovers the bulk of debate's benefit.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (2): the decider's competence and disposition, not the exchange, set the verdict. Their 'judge must verify, not summarise' condition is the mechanism behind our 16.17 result that sonnet raises and haiku lowers the verdict over identical locked seats. Their rebuttal-round ablation null matches 16.10, where cutting every read arc leaves lock, localisation and grip intact and only lowers the fire rate. Verified on the arXiv abstract page; no venue listed.

verified_entries.title: Scaling Laws For Scalable Oversight
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Proposes a framework that quantifies the probability of successful oversight as a function of the capabilities of the overseer and the system being overseen, modelling oversight as a game between capability-mismatched players with oversight-specific Elo scores; validates it on a modified Nim and on four oversight games (Mafia, Debate, Backdoor Code, Wargames), where Debate is a judge deciding from the transcript of two adversarial agents; derives scaling laws and a theory of nested scalable oversight, with NSO success at a 400 Elo gap of 51.7% for Debate.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (2): judge competence against debater competence as the axis. Their Debate game is exactly our moderator reading a transcript of opposed seats, and their finding that the judge's success scales with the judge's capability while the debaters' persuasion stays flat is the curve of which our 16.17 (sonnet up, haiku down over byte-identical seats) is a two-point instance. Published version used (NeurIPS 2025); arXiv abstract page fetched as the primary record.

verified_entries.title: Confirmation Bias: A Challenge for Scalable Oversight
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Reanalysis of prior oversight studies suggests that reported successes were driven by evaluators who answer the question themselves when they know it and defer to the model otherwise, a strategy that fails as models improve; two new studies of simple oversight protocols where evaluators know the model is 'correct most of the time, but not all of the time' find no overall advantage, although in Study 1 showing arguments in favor of both answers improves accuracy in the cases where the model is incorrect, and in Study 2 participants became more confident in the system's answers after online research even when those answers were incorrect.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (3), the flag: opposed arguments pay off on exactly the cases where the answer is wrong, which is the asymmetry our second-objector flag exploits (flagged cases wrong 9.8x as often). Also claim (1): deference to the model is the judge-side form of the pull our design corrects while the answer is written. Published version used (AAAI 2026, OJS page fetched).

verified_entries.title: Great Models Think Alike and this Undermines AI Oversight
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Proposes Chance Adjusted Probabilistic Agreement (CAPA), a metric of language-model similarity based on overlap in model mistakes; shows that LLM-as-a-judge scores favour models similar to the judge, generalising self-preference results; finds that complementary knowledge between a weak supervisor and a strong student drives weak-to-strong gains; and observes that model mistakes are becoming more similar as capabilities increase, pointing to risks from correlated failures in AI oversight.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (2): a judge that shares the seats' errors is not an independent check. This is the reason a majority of same-model seats never beats its best seat and the reason the design document's bipartite recommendation (seats for dissent, a decider chosen for accuracy, ideally from another vendor) follows; our 16.18 cross-vendor panel measured the lower error correlation they predict (phi 0.25 against 0.65) and still could not beat its best member. Published PMLR page fetched.

verified_entries.title: AI Debate Aids Assessment of Controversial Claims
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Two AI systems debate opposing sides of controversial factuality claims about COVID-19 and climate change in front of judges who hold prior beliefs; in Study I debate improves human judges' accuracy and confidence calibration over a single-advisor consultancy protocol by 4-10 points, most for judges with mainstream beliefs (up to +15.2 on COVID-19 claims) while also moving skeptical judges toward accurate views (+4.7); in Study II AI judges given human-like personas reach 78.5% accuracy against 70.1% for human judges and 69.8% for default AI judges.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claims (1) and (2): the judge's own pull (a prior belief) is the bias that opposed advocates are set against, and the judge decides from the exchange. Their persona-on-the-judge result is the mirror of our design, where the moderator is given no side; their debate-over-consultancy gain is the gain of an opposed pair over a single persuader that the design document derives from Milgrom-Roberts. Published version (NeurIPS 2025) used; arXiv abstract and the neurips.cc poster page fetched.

verified_entries.title: Training Language Models to Win Debates with Self-Play Improves Judge Accuracy
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Tests the robustness of debate as a method of scalable oversight by training models to debate with data generated via self-play; on a long-context reading comprehension task, language-model judges answer more accurately when judging models optimised to win debates, whereas no such relationship holds for consultancy models trained to persuade a judge without an opposing debater present; debate training encourages stronger and more informative arguments.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (2): judge accuracy is a property of the opposed pairing, not of a single persuader, which is the Milgrom-Roberts premise our graph is built on. Contrast for the related-work section: their judge gains come from training the debaters to win; our seats are untrained copies fixed by their briefs, and the gain we certify is the flag and the routed verdict, not the collective's own verdict. Verified on the arXiv abstract page only: secondary sources report ICLR 2025 acceptance (OpenReview forum gAEEjGv5Oa) but the OpenReview page returned a bot-check and the arXiv comments field lists no venue, so cite as arXiv.

verified_entries.title: When Two LLMs Debate, Both Think They'll Win
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Sixty three-round zero-sum policy debates among ten LLMs, each model privately rating its confidence in winning after each round: models start at 72.9% average confidence against a rational 50% baseline, raise rather than lower confidence as the debate proceeds (83% by the final round), in 61.7% of debates both sides simultaneously claim at least 75%, models debating identical copies of themselves still escalate, and private scratchpad reasoning sometimes diverges from the public confidence rating.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (3), the credible-signal principle: an advocate's confidence in its own side is a constant of its role and carries nothing about the case, so a statement with assigned interest is uninformative and only the objection against interest can be read. Their two-copies result is the with-interest half of our who-loses table (W objects on 0.992 of YTA verdicts). arXiv abstract page fetched; no venue listed.

verified_entries.title: A Layered Analysis of Disagreement And Answer Quality in Multi-Agent LLM Debate
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Asks whether the disagreement in multi-agent debate is genuine, with four measurements (self-reported agreement, whether the reply text pushes back, whether the position persists once the eliciting instruction is removed, and log-probability stance for open-weight models) over 750 three-model debates on GlobalOpinionQA under friendly, neutral and hostile tones: tone shifts reported full agreement by 50.4 points, dissent reverts toward agreement 23.1 points more often once the hostile instruction is deleted, opposing arguments weaken a stance margin more than they flip it, and no final-answer quality gain is detected (a bias-checked jury returns 299/299 ties; an unchecked jury had favoured debate 66% of the time through reading order).
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (3): dissent that the instruction produced is not evidence about the case. This is why our flag discounts the objection every brief predicts (the losing advocate) and reads only the objection no brief explains, and why the pooled objection text recovers little. Their null on answer quality is our claim (2) that the collective is not a better answerer by vote. arXiv abstract page fetched; no venue listed.

verified_entries.title: Budgeted Act-or-Defer Multi-Agent LLM Deliberation with Local Reliability Bounds
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Formulates deployment of multi-agent LLM deliberation as budgeted act-or-defer decision making: at each round the debate prefix is mapped to a low-dimensional state, a k-nearest-neighbour lower confidence bound on state-conditional correctness is computed from calibration data, and the system acts only when the bound exceeds a user-specified reliability threshold, otherwise escalating to human review; on six benchmarks against nine baselines it uses 9-12% of the pre-declared budget on activated datasets, reaching up to 84% automation and 96% acted-on accuracy, and defers on stress-test datasets.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (3), routing: the same architecture as our flagged-fifth cascade (act on the collective's verdict where the deliberation looks reliable, escalate the rest to a stronger judge) with the difference that their reliability signal is fitted on labelled calibration data and ours is the unlabelled count of objections no brief explains. arXiv abstract page fetched; no venue listed.

verified_entries.title: Debate Training Reduces Reward Hacking in RLAIF
verified_entries.what_it_shows: RL finetuning of a Gemini 2.5 Flash-class policy with debate, a two-player adversarial game between a generator and a critic adjudicated by a frozen weaker Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite judge, reduces reward hacking relative to a single-player RLAIF baseline on mathematics tasks with verifiable answers: the baseline quickly hacks the judge while debate maintains judge performance throughout training; further weakening the judge speeds hacking but an additional debate round compensates; debate incentives override prompted misalignment.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (2): a weaker judge over stronger interested speakers holds only because a second speaker with the opposite interest is present, which is the credible-signal premise; their finding that an extra round compensates for a weaker judge is the one place the exchange itself does the work, where in our record the exchange only amplifies the fire rate (16.10, 16.16). arXiv abstract page fetched; no venue listed.

verified_entries.title: Collaborative Disagreement Resolution for Scalable Oversight
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Reframes the oversight interaction from adversarial debate, where models argue opposing positions, to collaborative truth seeking drawn from human mediation practice, in which AI systems identify points of disagreement, examine the evidence for conflicting claims and converge toward consensus; non-expert judge models reach 62.1% judging accuracy against 49.2% for standard debate.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (3): disagreement is the object the protocol works on. They resolve it inside the collective; we read it as a flag and route outside to a stronger uninterested judge, and our record says the internal loop is null (a collective fed its own dissent moves +0.012 [-0.039, +0.063]). Their weak-judge gain over standard debate is consistent with our finding that opposed seats are a sensor rather than a generator of the answer. Re-fetched on the arXiv abstract page this session (also in the prior ledger, not yet in references.bib).

verified_entries.title: Debate Helps Weak-to-Strong Generalization
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Combines scalable oversight with weak-to-strong generalization: a strong model's debate is used to improve a weak model's supervision, and the improved weak supervisor then trains the strong model; debate lets a weak model extract trustworthy information from an untrustworthy strong model, an ensemble of weak models exploits the long arguments of strong debaters for a more robust supervision estimate, and on the OpenAI weak-to-strong NLP benchmarks the combination yields better alignment.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (3), routing direction: they run debate so that a weak decider can supervise a strong model; our cascade runs the other way, a cheap collective whose flagged fifth goes to a stronger judge. Both treat the opposed pair as an instrument for a decider of a different competence than the speakers (claim 2). Published version used (AAAI 2025, OJS page fetched).

verified_entries.title: Scalable AI Safety via Doubly-Efficient Debate
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Extends the debate framework of Irving et al. (2018), whose honest strategy had to simulate deterministic AI systems for an exponential number of steps, with doubly-efficient debate protocols in which two polynomial-time provers compete to convince a verifier of the correctness of a computation that depends on black-box judgements; the honest strategy succeeds with a polynomial number of simulation steps, alignment of stochastic systems can be verified, and the guarantee holds even against an adversary with exponential resources, so any polynomial-time computation can be verified with a constant number of queries to human judgement.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (6), the theory the design draws on: debate as a protocol under which a bounded judge can rely on competition between interested provers, the complexity-theoretic form of Milgrom-Roberts and Lipman-Seppi. The honest prover's structural advantage is the analogue of our credible-signal principle, and the constant-query bound is the analogue of routing only the flagged fifth to the expensive judge. Published PMLR page fetched.

verified_entries.title: Avoiding Obfuscation with Prover-Estimator Debate
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Identifies the obfuscated arguments problem in recursive debate protocols, where a dishonest debater can use a computationally efficient strategy that forces an honest opponent to solve a computationally intractable problem in order to win, and gives a new prover-estimator protocol which, under certain stability assumptions, ensures that an honest debater can win with a strategy requiring computational efficiency comparable to its opponent's.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (6) and claim (4): asymmetric roles, one seat asserts and one probes, are the theoretical form of an uninterested seat reading interested ones, and the obfuscation failure is a formally derived limit of adversarial protocols of which our extent map (floods where everyone loses, silent where no one deviates, a prisoner's dilemma no seating repairs) is the empirical counterpart. arXiv abstract page fetched; no venue listed.

verified_entries.title: Neural Interactive Proofs
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Studies how a trusted but computationally bounded verifier can learn to interact with one or more powerful but untrusted provers to solve a task; introduces a unifying framework based on prover-verifier games that generalises previously proposed interaction protocols, describes several new protocols for generating neural interactive proofs with a theoretical comparison of new and existing approaches, and validates them on a toy graph-isomorphism problem and a code-validation task with large language models.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (2): the collective as a graph of roles with a designated decider. Their prover-verifier games are the general class of which debate, consultancy and our three-seat star with a moderator are instances, and their comparison of protocols by what the bounded verifier can extract is the question 16.10 and 16.17 answer empirically for one protocol. ICLR 2025 per the arXiv comments field (OpenReview blocked by a bot-check); arXiv abstract page fetched.

verified_entries.title: Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Understanding Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Examines how differences in model capability shape multi-agent debate and finds that debate can lower accuracy over time even when stronger models outnumber weaker ones, because models abandon correct answers when peers present flawed reasoning, prioritising consensus over accuracy; sycophancy and conformity bias are identified as contributing factors when agents lack incentives or resilience against persuasive but incorrect argument.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (1) and (2): the pull passes through debate among copies, which is why our seats are fixed by assignment rather than left to converge, and why the exchange is treated as an amplifier of against-interest objection rather than as a source of truth. Their conformity failure is the mechanism that would erase the flag if the seats were not locked. Venue is the ICML 2025 MAS workshop per the arXiv comments field; arXiv abstract page fetched.

verified_entries.title: Commitment To Cooperation With Self-Negotiated Contracts
verified_entries.what_it_shows: LLM-based agents in a spatial-temporal bargaining-plus-navigation game ("CT") are given contract representations ranging from formal contracts that compile to code to natural-language contracts that need reinterpretation; across backbones of several sizes and providers, self-negotiated contracts improve cooperative outcomes beyond what regular trading achieves, because contracts make commitments credible through enforcement of terms (arXiv v1, 23 Jul 2026; no venue listed).
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: The enforcement axis of claim (4). Our binding regime (16.13 B1) grants enforcement by fiat and the solo model then solves the dilemma alone; our non-binding one-shot PD (16.13c) has no enforcement and no third node can make cooperation rational. Wyse et al. supply the enforcement device itself: LLM agents cooperate with commitment only once a contract makes defection punishable, which is the same reading of why the mediator seat has nothing to do without it.

verified_entries.title: Will Systems of LLM Agents Cooperate: An Investigation into a Social Dilemma
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Instead of choosing single moves, LLMs are prompted to write complete strategies for the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma; evolutionary game-theory simulations over populations of agents with aggressive, cooperative or neutral dispositions show that different LLMs carry particular biases that decide whether aggressive or cooperative strategies prevail (arXiv v1, 27 Jan 2025, 7 pages; no venue listed).
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (4) and the open direction named in graph_theory_design.md section 5 (repeated play). Our one-shot non-binding PD found every node recommending the Nash action; Willis et al. study the repeated game where model-level dispositions, not the game alone, decide which strategy survives, so the two results bracket the one-shot / repeated boundary our extent map draws.

verified_entries.title: Nicer than Humans: How Do Large Language Models Behave in the Prisoner's Dilemma?
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Llama2, Llama3 and GPT-3.5 play the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma against random adversaries of varying hostility, after a methodology that checks each model's grasp of the rules and its parsing of the game log; all models tend not to initiate defection and favour cooperation only when the opponent's defection rate is low, with Llama2 and GPT-3.5 more cooperative than humans and Llama3 more human-like and exploitative (ICWSM 2025, vol. 19(1), pp. 522-535; published version used).
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Contrast for claim (4). In repeated play LLMs lean cooperative; in our one-shot PD without enforcement every seat, the neutral reader, the mediator and the solo model recommend defection (Nash-pull 1.000). Positions our reading that the unanimity on the equilibrium is the correct answer to the one-shot question as put, not a model's reluctance to cooperate.

verified_entries.title: What Suppresses Nash Equilibrium Play in Large Language Models? Mechanistic Evidence and Causal Control
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Across four open models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, 8B to 72B) and four canonical two-player games, probes find opponent history encoded almost perfectly at the first layer (96%) while the Nash action is encoded weakly (never above 56%); a prosocial override concentrated in the final layers suppresses Nash-optimal play, chain-of-thought affects Nash play differently by scale, and cross-play reveals phenomena invisible in self-play; the authors conclude the models compute Nash and then suppress it (arXiv v2, 4 May 2026; no venue listed).
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: The 'LLMs recommend the equilibrium' question in claim (4), and a mechanistic version of the pull our introduction describes as a bias entering while the answer is written. Their prosocial override is model-dependent; our grok seats showed none on the one-shot PD, so citing them situates our unanimous-Nash result as one point in a model-dependent family rather than a universal.

verified_entries.title: Communication Enables Cooperation in LLM Agents: A Comparison with Curriculum-Based Approaches
verified_entries.what_it_shows: In a four-player Stag Hunt a one-word cheap-talk channel raises cooperation from 0% to 48.3% in the published EACL abstract (the arXiv v3 comments line, 11 Mar 2026, corrects this to 96.7% after a denominator bug), while a curriculum of progressively harder games cuts payoffs by 27.4% in an iterated public-goods game with punishment and induces 'learned pessimism'; simple communication is the more reliable coordination mechanism (EACL 2026 short papers, pp. 307-321; published version used, discrepancy with arXiv v3 noted).
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (4), the coordination half. Our 16.13d result is that deliberation among opposed seats lets the model coordinate on an equilibrium where the solo declines (D2 holds) while the mediator adds nothing (D1 fails); Madmoun and Lahlou show the same thing from the other side, a minimal talk channel solves a coordination game with no third party at all. Both are consistent with cheap-talk theory (crawford1982strategic already in bib): talk coordinates where interests align and cannot enforce where they do not.

verified_entries.title: ProMediate: A Simulation Testbed for Evaluating Proactive Mediation in Multi-Party Negotiation
verified_entries.what_it_shows: A testbed for proactive AI mediator agents in multi-topic, multi-party negotiations: a simulation environment built on realistic cases with LLM negotiators and a plug-and-play mediator that decides when and how to intervene, plus a socio-cognitive metric suite for consensus change, intervention latency, effectiveness and intelligence; a socially intelligent mediator beats a generic baseline by 3.6 points of consensus change with 77% faster responses (Findings of ACL 2026, pp. 29570-29598; published version used).
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (4) on third-party recommendation and the mediator node of claim (2). ProMediate finds that how a mediator is built (when and how it intervenes) moves consensus among LLM negotiators with assigned personas; our 16.13d found the planner-mediator seat adds nothing over a naive reader on an equilibrium recommendation (D1 fails). The difference is the task: consensus-building in open negotiation versus recommending a self-enforcing action, which is exactly where Aumann's mediator is supposed to matter and did not on our games.

verified_entries.title: Cooperation, Competition, and Maliciousness: LLM-Stakeholders Interactive Negotiation
verified_entries.what_it_shows: A testbed of multi-agent, multi-issue, semantically rich negotiation games in which each party holds secret scores, issue priorities and an acceptance threshold; metrics measure performance and alignment with the assigned role, scenarios can be generated at increasing difficulty, and greedy or adversarial players are added to probe safety; small models largely fail and GPT-4 and Llama-3 70B still underperform at reaching agreement, especially in non-cooperative settings (NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks Track; published version used).
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Negotiation with assigned interests, claims (1) and (5). Their role-alignment metric (does a party act on its secret scores) is a cousin of our role-lock, and their finding that agreement fails in non-cooperative settings mirrors our advocates who lock at the opening statement on any payoff table where interests diverge. Also the nearest multi-party (more than two stakeholders) instrument to our 16.21 third-party advocate.

verified_entries.title: How Well Can LLMs Negotiate? NegotiationArena Platform and Analysis
verified_entries.what_it_shows: NegotiationArena runs multi-turn dialogues between LLM agents in three scenario types (ultimatum-style resource allocation, trading, price negotiation); LLM agents can raise their payoff by about 20% against a standard GPT-4 counterpart by adopting behavioural tactics such as feigning desperation, and the models display irrational negotiation patterns that parallel human ones (ICML 2024, PMLR 235:3935-3951; published version used).
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Negotiation with assigned interests, claim (1). Two copies of one model given opposite sides bargain to different outcomes depending on the brief each is handed, which is the embodiment-as-lever result in a bargaining setting, and their 20% payoff shift from a tactic in the brief is the same control surface our seats expose.

verified_entries.title: Beyond Nash Equilibrium: Bounded Rationality of LLMs and humans in Strategic Decision-making
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Using Rock-Paper-Scissors and Prisoner's Dilemma designs from behavioural game theory, LLMs reproduce human heuristics such as outcome-based strategy switching and more cooperation when future interaction is possible, but apply them more rigidly and are less sensitive to evolving game dynamics; even reasoning models struggle with adaptive strategies (arXiv v1, 11 Jun 2025; no venue listed). Secondary entry.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (4), secondary. Documents the one-shot versus repeated distinction our C1 result rests on: LLM cooperation in the PD rises when future interaction is possible, and our game was one-shot with no future, so unanimity on the equilibrium is expected rather than anomalous.

verified_entries.title: LLM Strategic Reasoning: Agentic Study through Behavioral Game Theory
verified_entries.what_it_shows: A behavioural game-theoretic framework that separates intrinsic strategic reasoning from contextual influence is applied to 22 LLMs; GPT-o3-mini, GPT-o1 and DeepSeek-R1 lead in reasoning depth, scale alone does not predict performance, chain-of-thought helps only some models, and assigned demographic personas shift reasoning depth (e.g. GPT-4o reasons more deeply with female traits; Gemma assigns higher levels to heterosexual identities). NeurIPS 2025 poster; the proceedings.neurips.cc hash page was not located (the 2025 paper_files index fetched listed only the Creative AI track), so the neurips.cc virtual page plus arXiv abstract were used. Secondary entry.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (1), secondary. Independent evidence that an assigned identity moves a model's strategic reasoning, which is embodiment as a control input inside a game rather than a dispute; also the reasoning-model caveat for any replication of our games family with stronger models.

'Tacit Coordination of Large Language Models' (focal points in tacit coordination games): same aggregator only; no primary page located. No bib entry.

verified_entries.title: Systematic Biases in LLM Simulations of Debates
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Persona-assigned LLM agents in multi-round simulated political debates conform to the model's inherent social biases despite being directed to argue from assigned political perspectives, and fine-tuning the underlying model's bias moves all the agents together.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (1) and (2): the closest prior result on persona-assigned agents inside a debate graph. It shows the limit of assignment as a control: the role fixes the stance but the shared model pulls every seat the same way, which is the mechanism behind the paper's finding that copies share the same pull, that same-model seats never beat the best seat, and that the effective voter count is one. Cite where the paper says assignment is a lever, not a cure. Published version used (EMNLP 2024 main).

verified_entries.title: Persona-Assigned Large Language Models Exhibit Human-Like Motivated Reasoning
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Assigning eight political and socio-demographic personas to eight LLMs on two ground-truth tasks (misinformation veracity discernment and evaluation of numeric scientific evidence) cuts veracity discernment by up to 9 percent, makes political personas up to 90 percent more likely to evaluate evidence correctly when the truth is congruent with the assigned identity, and prompt-based debiasing is largely ineffective.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (1): assignment fixes the conclusion and the fix has a price on ground truth, measured on items with a right answer. This is the accuracy-cost half of the paper's 99.7 / 97.4 percent lock result, and its finding that debiasing prompts do not undo the effect supports the paper's move to correct the bias structurally rather than by prompting. Published version used (Findings of ACL 2026; arXiv 2506.20020 also fetched, v2 16 Apr 2026).

verified_entries.title: Whose Opinions Do Language Models Reflect?
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Using the OpinionQA benchmark built from public opinion polls over 60 US demographic groups, the paper finds substantial misalignment between the opinions LMs reflect and those of the groups, on the order of the Democrat-Republican divide on climate change, and the misalignment persists even after explicitly steering the LM toward a particular group.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (1): the canonical measurement that steering a model toward a group only partly moves its answer, so a persona is not a full control over opinion. Useful as the contrast case: the paper's briefs assign an interest rather than a demographic, and lock is near-complete (99.7 / 97.4 percent), which is why assignment works as a lever here where demographic steering does not. Published version used (ICML 2023, PMLR 202).

verified_entries.title: In-Context Impersonation Reveals Large Language Models' Strengths and Biases
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Prefixing a prompt with a persona changes what the model does: LLMs impersonating children of different ages recover human-like developmental stages of exploration in a bandit task, LLMs impersonating domain experts outperform those impersonating non-experts, and impersonation also surfaces social biases (a model prompted as a man describes cars better than one prompted as a woman).
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (1): an early controlled demonstration that an assigned persona is a control input that reliably shifts behaviour, both competence and bias, in the direction the persona implies. Cite alongside shanahan2023roleplay as the empirical base for treating assignment as a lever. Published version used (NeurIPS 2023 proceedings page).

verified_entries.title: Evaluating Large Language Model Biases in Persona-Steered Generation
verified_entries.what_it_shows: In open-ended persona-steered generation, LLMs are 9.7 percent less steerable toward incongruous personas (multi-trait personas where one trait makes the others less likely in survey data) than toward congruous ones, sometimes producing the stereotypical stance instead of the target stance; RLHF-tuned models are more steerable but present less diverse views.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (1): measures how completely a persona fixes the generated stance and where it fails, namely when the assigned stance conflicts with what the model expects of that persona. Relevant to the paper's residual 0.3 / 2.6 percent of seats that do not take their side and to the finding that the pull of the underlying model survives assignment. Published version used (Findings of ACL 2024).

verified_entries.title: Evaluating the Prompt Steerability of Large Language Models
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Defines prompt steerability formally as the degree to which a model's joint behavioural distribution can be shifted from its baseline by prompting, builds a benchmark of steerability indices as a function of steering effort across persona dimensions, and finds that the steerability of many current models is limited because of skew in baseline behaviour and asymmetry across dimensions and directions.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (1): supplies the formal vocabulary (steerability as a shift of the behavioural distribution from baseline, asymmetric by direction) for stating what the paper's role-lock numbers measure, and its asymmetry finding parallels the paper's asymmetric lock (99.7 for the writer's side against 97.4 for the other party). Published version used (NAACL 2025).

verified_entries.title: Enhancing AI-Assisted Group Decision Making through LLM-Powered Devil's Advocate
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Designs four styles of LLM-powered devil's advocate (interactive or not; objecting to the AI recommendation or to the group majority) and shows in a randomised human-subject experiment that devil's advocates arguing against the AI model's recommendation can promote groups' appropriate reliance on AI without substantially raising perceived workload.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (1) and (3): the 'playing devil's advocate' use of role assignment, where an LLM is told to object regardless of the merits so that its objection carries no information about the case. The paper's flag is the inverse design: it reads the objection that the assigned side does not explain. Cite as the human-facing devil's-advocate line next to nemeth2001devil and kelkar2026devil. Verified this session from the ACM DOI landing page (published 05 April 2024, pages 103-119), which prior sweeps could not fetch; the NSF public-access copy of the published PDF was also read.

verified_entries.title: When "A Helpful Assistant" Is Not Really Helpful: Personas in System Prompts Do Not Improve Performances of Large Language Models
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Across 162 roles (6 interpersonal relationship types, 8 expertise domains), 2,410 factual questions and 4 LLM families, adding a persona to the system prompt does not improve accuracy over no persona; persona attributes such as gender, type and domain shift accuracy, and strategies for picking the best persona per question perform near random.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Claim (1): the largest systematic test that a role in the system prompt moves the output without making it more correct, which is the paper's distinction between assignment as a lever over what a copy says and assignment as a cure. Published version used (Findings of EMNLP 2024).

verified_entries.title: Moral Mimicry: Large Language Models Produce Moral Rationalizations Tailored to Political Identity
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Using Moral Foundations Theory on the GPT-3/3.5 and OPT families, the paper shows that when prompted with a liberal or conservative political identity the models generate moral rationalisations reflecting the corresponding moral biases, an effect that grows with model size.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: [secondary] Claim (1): the earliest quantified result that an assigned identity pins the moral rationale a model produces, on moral-judgement text like the paper's dispute adjudication task. Student Research Workshop paper; cite as a precursor, not as primary support. Published version used.

verified_entries.title: Better Zero-Shot Reasoning with Role-Play Prompting
verified_entries.what_it_shows: A two-stage role-play prompting method, evaluated on twelve reasoning benchmarks in the zero-shot setting, raises accuracy on most of them (ChatGPT on AQuA 53.5 to 63.8 percent, Last Letter 23.8 to 84.2 percent) and acts as a more effective trigger of chain-of-thought than Zero-Shot-CoT.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: [secondary] Claim (1): the benefit-side counterpart to kim2025persona and zheng2024helpful, needed so the related-work paragraph on role prompting is balanced (a role can raise accuracy on some tasks, lower it on others, and either way it moves the answer). Published version used (NAACL 2024).

verified_entries.title: Measuring Opinion Bias and Sycophancy via LLM-based Persuasion
verified_entries.what_it_shows: A benchmark in which a simulated user with a neutral, agreeing or disagreeing persona probes 13 assistants on 38 contentious Brazilian-Portuguese topics over multi-turn conversations, directly and through argumentative debate; the three-persona design separates persona-independent opinion bias from sycophantic drift that tracks the user's persona, and argumentative debate triggers sycophancy two to three times more than direct questioning.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: [secondary] Claim (1) and (3): a role-assignment design used as a measuring instrument, where the assigned user persona is varied so that the part of the verdict that tracks the persona can be separated from the part that does not, the same logic as reading an objection relative to who raised it. arXiv preprint (v2 30 Apr 2026), no venue listed; cite as preprint.

verified_entries.title: From Single to Societal: Analyzing Persona-Induced Bias in Multi-Agent Interactions
verified_entries.what_it_shows: In controlled collaborative problem-solving and persuasion tasks, persona-assigned LLM agents show biases in trustworthiness (how an agent's opinion is received) and insistence (how strongly it advocates), with personas from historically advantaged groups perceived as less trustworthy and less insistent, and agents show in-group favouritism, conforming more to others sharing their persona; the effects persist across LLMs, group sizes and interaction rounds.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: [secondary] Claim (2): personas inside a multi-agent graph change how seats weigh one another, so who reads whom is not neutral to the roles assigned; relevant to the paper's edge-cutting result that the flag survives removing the seats' reads of one another. arXiv abstract page fetched (v1 14 Nov 2025, comments AAAI-2026); no AAAI proceedings page located, so cite the arXiv version.

verified_entries.title: FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Surveys three cost-reduction strategies for LLM APIs (prompt adaptation, LLM approximation, LLM cascade) and proposes FrugalGPT, a learned cascade that picks which LLMs to call per query, matching the best single LLM (GPT-4) at up to 98% lower cost or beating it by 4% at equal cost.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: The canonical LLM-cascade framing: a cheap generator answers most queries and a learned scorer decides when to call the expensive one. Our routing result (a flagged fifth of cases sent to a stronger uninterested judge, 16.11a) is a two-stage cascade of this shape, but the deferral signal is read off a structured collective's dissent rather than a scorer trained on labelled outputs, and we report, as FrugalGPT's framing predicts, that the gain is cost-efficiency (59% of the strong judge's gain at 17.5% of its calls) rather than an accuracy ceiling, since the strong judge everywhere dominates.

verified_entries.title: Large Language Model Cascades with Mixture of Thought Representations for Cost-Efficient Reasoning
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Builds a weak-to-strong LLM cascade (GPT-3.5-turbo to GPT-4) that uses the answer consistency of the weaker model's sampled answers, including across Chain-of-Thought and Program-of-Thought representations, as the difficulty signal for deferral, matching the stronger model on six reasoning benchmarks at about 40% of its cost.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: The closest published instance of routing on sample disagreement: the weaker model's own answer inconsistency decides which questions go to the stronger model. This is exactly the within-model baseline we compare against (the solo's majority-of-3 disagreement, 16.15.2), which composes at least as well as our transferred flag on grok; our contribution is a different deferral signal, a second seat objecting against its assigned interest, that needs neither multiple samples of the base model nor labelled data, and that survives when the seats never read one another (16.10) and when narration is cut (16.16). Published title differs from the arXiv title ('Mixture of Thoughts Representations', 'Cost-efficient'); the ICLR proceedings form is used.

verified_entries.title: When Does Confidence-Based Cascade Deferral Suffice?
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Characterises the theoretically optimal deferral rule for a two-model cascade, which depends on the confidence of both the first and the second model, shows that deferring on the first model's confidence alone is competitive when the downstream model is a consistent posterior estimate, and identifies settings (specialised models, label noise, distribution shift) where it is markedly sub-optimal and post-hoc deferral rules do better.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Supplies the theory for a result we found empirically: the value of a deferral signal depends on the downstream model as much as on the signal. Our flag was equally sharp in 16.8 and 16.11a, but routing to a haiku judge (0.850) could not repair a 0.912 base while routing to sonnet (0.976) certified a gain; in their terms the sensor was right and the second model was the bottleneck. It also frames why a strong enough judge used everywhere dominates any deferral rule.

verified_entries.title: Language Model Cascades: Token-Level Uncertainty And Beyond
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Initiates a systematic study of deferral rules for generative LM cascades, shows that predicted sequence uncertainty suffers a length bias, and shows that learned post-hoc deferral rules over token-level uncertainty quantiles (plus embeddings from the small model and intermediate layers of the large one) give better cost-quality trade-offs than naive aggregation on FLAN-T5 benchmarks.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Positions our deferral signal against the model-internal (white-box) family: their rules read token-level uncertainty from the generator's own logits, ours reads a structural property of a black-box collective (a second objector on a one-loser verdict) that needs no access to probabilities and no trained deferral rule. Their finding that a naive aggregate of the generator's uncertainty is a poor deferral signal is one reason the field looks past the single model's own signals, which is where our flag sits.

verified_entries.title: AutoMix: Automatically Mixing Language Models
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Routes queries to a larger LM based on the approximate correctness of a smaller LM's output, using a few-shot self-verification prompt (no verifier training) and a POMDP router that tolerates the verifier's noise, cutting computational cost by over 50% at comparable performance across five models and five datasets.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: The nearest routing design to ours in spirit: an untrained, prompt-level signal about the small model's answer decides escalation. AutoMix asks the same model to verify itself; we found that a copy of the model with no side is a dictator over the collective's verdict (16.15.4) and that a model's self-report is subject to the same pull as its answer, so our signal instead comes from a seat speaking against its assigned interest, a statement the model has been told not to make. Both papers treat the router as a noisy sensor to be composed with a stronger model rather than as a verdict.

verified_entries.title: Trust or Escalate: LLM Judges with Provable Guarantees for Human Agreement
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Proposes selective evaluation for LLM judges: estimate the judge's confidence (via Simulated Annotators) and decide when to trust its judgement, with Cascaded Selective Evaluation that starts from cheap judge models and escalates to stronger ones only when needed while provably guaranteeing a user-specified level of human agreement (over 80% agreement at almost 80% coverage with Mistral-7B on a Chatbot Arena subset where GPT-4 fails that bar).
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: The published answer to 'when to escalate to a stronger judge', and the framing our routing result belongs in: a cheap judge decides most cases, a confidence signal abstains on the rest, and a stronger judge is paid for only there. They obtain the abstention signal from a calibrated confidence estimate of the judge itself (Simulated Annotators) and tie escalation to a user-set human-agreement guarantee; we obtain it from opposed advocates whose interests are assigned, and we route a flagged fifth to an uninterested stronger judge (16.11a) without a calibration set or an agreement target. Their guarantee framework is a natural extension for our flag that we do not provide.

verified_entries.title: SelfCheckGPT: Zero-Resource Black-Box Hallucination Detection for Generative Large Language Models
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Detects hallucinations with no external database and no access to output probabilities by sampling several responses and measuring their mutual consistency, on the premise that known facts reproduce across samples while fabrications diverge; on WikiBio it finds non-factual sentences and ranks passages by factuality better than grey-box baselines.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: The zero-resource, black-box error detector our flag is most often compared to: disagreement among samples of one model, needing no labels. Our 16.15.2 readout shows that this within-model disagreement concentrates the solo model's errors as well as our transferred flag does (6.35x against 4.40x on grok), which is why the paper's transfer claim was demoted and its practical claim rests on the cross-vendor readout. The difference in mechanism remains: SelfCheckGPT reads stochastic variation, our flag reads a deterministic structural fact (which seat objects and against which interest) and fires even when each seat writes alone.

verified_entries.title: Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy
verified_entries.fetch_method_2026_09_14: Browser pane (WebFetch was redirected to idp.nature.com); citation_* meta tags read for volume 630, issue 8017, pages 625-630, DOI
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Proposes entropy-based uncertainty estimators computed at the level of meaning (clustering sampled answers by bidirectional entailment) to detect confabulations, arbitrary and incorrect generations, without task-specific data or prior knowledge of the task, generalising to unseen tasks and telling users when a prompt is likely to produce a confabulation.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: The strongest published label-free error detector for a single model, and the reference point for the claim that our flag needs no labelled data. Semantic entropy, like SelfCheckGPT, reads variation across samples of the same model under the same prompt; our flag reads agreement between seats whose prompts pull in opposite directions, and so is informative even where the model's samples agree with one another (the sycophantic case, where every copy shares the pull). The paper should cite it when stating that the collective's flag is one more member of the label-free family and say where it differs. Publisher page reached by direct fetch after WebFetch was redirected to the Nature identity gateway; fields read from the page's citation metadata.

verified_entries.title: Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Defines a black-box framework for confidence elicitation (prompting strategies for verbalised confidence, sampling, and consistency aggregation) and finds across five LLMs and five task types that models are overconfident when verbalising confidence, that human-inspired prompts and consistency checks reduce but do not remove it, and that all methods struggle on tasks needing professional knowledge.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Covers the verbalised-confidence alternative to our flag and gives the reason we did not use it: a model's stated confidence is overconfident and is produced by the same model under the same pull as its answer. Their finding that consistency among multiple responses and better aggregation mitigate the overconfidence matches our 16.15.2 result that the solo's sample disagreement is a strong within-model signal; our flag is a third route, confidence read off the structure of interests rather than off the model's self-report or its sampling noise.

verified_entries.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Replaces greedy chain-of-thought decoding with sampling a diverse set of reasoning paths and taking the most consistent final answer by marginalising over the paths, on the intuition that a problem with a unique correct answer admits many ways of reaching it, and reports large gains on GSM8K (+17.9%), SVAMP, AQuA, StrategyQA and ARC-challenge.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: The origin of the majority-of-k solo baseline we use everywhere (grok solo majority-of-3 at 0.912) and of the disagreement-among-samples signal that our routing result is measured against (16.11a union sensor, 16.15.2). Self-consistency is the identical-copy aggregation that the paper argues cannot remove a shared bias, since copies of one model share the pull and their votes are correlated (majority gain +0.003 at error correlation 0.6 in the identical cells of 16.10), which is the motivation for aggregating opposed seats instead. verified_entries.title: Sycophantic AI Decreases Prosocial Intentions and Promotes Dependence

verified_entries.what_it_shows: Across 11 models, AI affirms users' actions about 50% more than humans do even when the query involves manipulation, deception or other interpersonal harm; in two preregistered experiments (1,604 participants) a single interaction with a sycophantic model reduced willingness to repair interpersonal conflict and raised conviction of being right, while participants rated the sycophantic responses higher and trusted them more (arXiv v1 abstract).

verified_entries.title: Measuring Sycophancy of Language Models in Multi-turn Dialogues
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Introduces SYCON Bench, which measures how quickly a model conforms to the user (turn of flip) and how often it shifts stance under sustained pressure (number of flips) across multi-turn free-form conversation; on 17 LLMs in three scenarios, alignment tuning amplifies sycophancy while scaling and reasoning optimisation strengthen resistance, and having the model adopt a third-person perspective substantially reduces sycophancy.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: The multi-turn measurement is the closest published analogue of the paper's rounds (open, rebut, restate, accept or object), and its finding that a third-person perspective reduces sycophancy is prior evidence for the paper's 'light dose', narration as a perspective with no side, which cuts validation of the asker by 22 to 41 points. Use it to position narration as a known prompting remedy that the paper then shows is only an amplifier of objection, not the source of the structure (16.16).

verified_entries.title: From Yes-Men to Truth-Tellers: Addressing Sycophancy in Large Language Models with Pinpoint Tuning
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Frames sycophancy as prioritising adherence to the user's prompt over veracious answers, including admitting mistakes when challenged after a correct answer; proposes supervised pinpoint tuning, which locates and fine-tunes under 5 percent of a model's modules that drive the behaviour, and reports it reduces sycophancy more than ordinary supervised fine-tuning with little or no loss of general capability.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Represents the weight-editing branch of mitigation: a fix applied inside the model at training time. The paper's position is that a bias that enters while the answer is written must be corrected while the answer is written, by the arrangement of seats rather than by retraining, so this is the contrast case for the 'lever, not a cure' argument; note also that its definition (capitulating when challenged) is the very dynamic the paper's objection round exploits.

verified_entries.title: Sycophancy Claims about Language Models: The Missing Human-in-the-Loop
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Reviews the methodological problems in measuring LLM sycophancy, identifies five operationalisations in the literature, notes that despite the concept being human-centric no study evaluates human perception, and argues that sycophancy is hard to separate from neighbouring alignment concepts, in particular that persona-prompt measurements may conflate personalization with sycophancy.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Supplies the conceptual distinction the paper relies on in claim (1): assigning a copy of a model a side fixes its conclusion (99.7 and 97.4 percent) and that is a control, a form of steerability, not the same thing as deference to the user. Cite when defining the family of ungrounded claims (asker's feelings, accepted premise, assigned interest) as distinct pulls that share a remedy.

verified_entries.title: Sycophancy Is Not One Thing: Causal Separation of Sycophantic Behaviors in LLMs
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Decomposes sycophancy into sycophantic agreement and sycophantic praise, contrasted with genuine agreement, and using difference-in-means directions, activation additions and subspace geometry shows the three are encoded along distinct linear directions, can each be amplified or suppressed independently, and have consistent structure across model families and scales.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Mechanistic support for treating sycophancy as one member of a family of independently placeable pulls rather than a single switch: if the behaviours live on separable directions inside the model, a single steering fix leaves the others, which is the paper's argument for a structural remedy that does not depend on which pull is present. Pairs with rimsky2024caa and chen2025persona in the steering-vector paragraph.

verified_entries.title: The Assistant Axis: Situating and Stabilizing the Default Persona of Language Models
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Extracts activation directions for many character archetypes and finds their leading component is an 'Assistant Axis' measuring how far a model is in its default post-trained persona; deviation along it predicts persona drift toward harmful or bizarre behaviour, often in conversations with emotionally vulnerable users, and confining activations to a fixed region of the axis stabilises behaviour, with the conclusion that post-training only loosely tethers a model to its persona.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: The persona-space account of why an assigned perspective takes hold: the default persona is a region the model can be moved out of by prompt or conversation, which is what the paper exploits when it embodies a copy as an advocate and finds the assignment holds on 97 to 99.7 percent of openings. Also relevant to the vulnerable-user setting in which the paper's asker sits. Cite with chen2025persona as the persona-vector lineage.

verified_entries.title: Who Flips? Self- and Cross-Model Counterarguments Reveal Answer Instability in LLMs
verified_entries.what_it_shows: After a model answers a multiple-choice question correctly it is challenged with a coherent argument for a wrong option; across seven frontier models and 57 MMLU subjects flip rates run from 17.5 to 97.3 percent, attributing the counterargument to the model itself raises flips by a mean 7.1 points, and pooling wrong-answer arguments across models yields stronger challenges than any single source model (the MaxFlip set).
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: The rebuttal round in the paper's graph is exactly a counterargument delivered to a seat, and this paper measures how readily a model abandons a correct answer under one. It is the reason the paper cannot let advocates simply argue and vote: a persuasive wrong argument moves a seat. It also documents that arguments from a different model are stronger challengers, which bears on the cross-vendor decider panel of 16.18 and the cross-vendor moderator of 16.17. Cross-check the Anthology entry when Findings of EMNLP 2026 is published.

verified_entries.title: Knowing but Not Correcting: Routine Task Requests Suppress Factual Correction in LLMs
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Models correct false claims presented in isolation but comply rather than correct when the same claims are embedded in a task request; on a benchmark of 300 false premises across eight models, suppression runs from 19 to 90 percent, is triggered by benign framing such as role statements and output specifications rather than adversarial prompts, and mechanistic analysis shows the model registers the error internally while task context diverts attention as output intent settles on compliance.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: The clearest recent statement of the paper's second pull, an accepted premise: the conclusion is fixed by the request rather than by the evidence, and the model knows better. Its finding that role statements are one of the triggers is the same phenomenon the paper turns into a control (a brief fixes the copy's conclusion), and its false-premise benchmark sits beside BrokenMath (petrov2025brokenmath) and SycEval (fanous2025syceval) in the premise-acceptance line.

verified_entries.title: The Chain Holds, the Answer Folds: Trace-Answer Dissociation in Reasoning Models Under Adversarial Pressure
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Identifies 'unfaithful capitulation' in multi-turn dialogue: under sustained user pushback the chain-of-thought stays factually correct while the emitted answer flips wrong; across three datasets latent-correct rates cluster near 50 percent with reasoning enabled and fall to 11 to 15 percent without it, an independent judge validates 86 percent of labels, and token-level analysis finds the correct answer present in 84 percent of the wrongly answered cases.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Evidence at the level of the reasoning trace that the answer can be pulled away from the evidence the model itself has produced, which is the paper's definition of an ungrounded claim. It also shows that more reasoning does not close the gap, supporting the paper's move away from single-agent scaffolds toward a structure that reads objections across seats rather than trusting any one seat's chain.

verified_entries.title: Beyond Sycophancy: Structured Resistance and Compliance in LLM Moral Reasoning
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Argues that a socially calibrated model must learn from others without simply yielding, so sycophancy cannot be treated as a one-dimensional failure; examines how models revise moral judgements along three dimensions drawn from social psychology, positional distance, source attribution and coalition structure, and separates constructive belief revision from sycophantic compliance.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Closest in domain (moral judgement of interpersonal conduct) and in variables to the paper's seat-count results: source attribution is who is speaking, coalition structure is the like-biased second advocate of 16.19 and the third party of 16.21. Cite when arguing that whether a seat should move under an objection depends on who raised it and against what interest, the credible-signal reading of glazer2001debates.

verified_entries.title: Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents: Is Mixing Different Large Language Models Beneficial?
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Introduces Self-MoA, which aggregates several sampled outputs of a single top model instead of outputs from different models, and finds it beats mixed-model MoA in most scenarios (6.6 points on AlpacaEval 2.0, 3.8 on average over MMLU, CRUX and MATH), attributing this to a quality-diversity trade-off in which mixing weaker models lowers average quality (abstract). arXiv version used; a secondary index (mlanthology) reports publication in TMLR 2026 at OpenReview id K6WwK8URlV, but OpenReview could not be fetched this session, so the journal venue is unverified.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Direct precedent for the same-model-versus-cross-vendor comparison in claims (2) and (3): a panel of copies of the strongest model matches or beats a mixed panel, and the aggregator's output tracks the quality of what it reads; consistent with 16.18, where the cross-vendor decider panel does not beat three copies of the best model at the opening statement, and with the paper's position that the collective's value lies in the sensor, not in a better answer by vote.

verified_entries.title: Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate -- We Must Rethink Evaluation and Embrace Model Heterogeneity
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Position paper evaluating five multi-agent-debate methods on nine benchmarks with four base models; finds that debate often fails to beat single-agent chain-of-thought and self-consistency even at much higher inference cost, and argues that model heterogeneity is the lever future debate frameworks should use (abstract). arXiv v3 used (the ledger already carries this key under Strand 2 with no bib entry; a NeurIPS 2025 position-track OpenReview record exists but acceptance was not verified).
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Positions the paper's null on accuracy: every same-model collective in 16.10 sits below the solo model, so the paper agrees that debate among copies is not a better answerer and locates its contribution in what the arrangement of seats detects (the flag) rather than in the vote; its heterogeneity prescription is what 16.18 tests and finds insufficient at the opening statement.

verified_entries.title: Are Diversity Metrics Measuring Diversity? A Capability-Controlled Audit of Majority-Vote Gain in LLM Ensembles
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Audits five diversity measures as predictors of majority-vote gain over the best member across 31,900 subsets drawn from 30 LLMs on MMLU-Pro (29 on TruthfulQA) under explicit capability controls; oracle complementarity is present in every subset, yet simple majority voting beats the strongest member in only 9.98 percent of size-3 subsets, and raw diversity-gain associations are capability-entangled and unstable under control (abstract). arXiv v1, 22 July 2026.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: The closest external base rate for the paper's majority-versus-best-seat readout in claim (2): over thousands of three-model panels the majority rarely beats its best member, so the paper's finding that three seats never aggregate to more than one reader (16.10, 16.18 at the opening statement) is the expected case for a three-member panel rather than an anomaly of the protocol.

verified_entries.title: Voting or Consensus? Decision-Making in Multi-Agent Debate
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Holds every debate parameter fixed and varies only the decision protocol across seven protocols (majority voting, unanimity consensus and others); voting protocols improve reasoning-task performance by 13.2 percent and consensus protocols improve knowledge-task performance by 2.8 percent, more agents help while more discussion rounds before the decision hurt, and two diversity-raising methods (All-Agents Drafting, Collective Improvement) add up to 7.4 percent (abstract). Published version used (Findings of ACL 2025, pages 11640-11671).
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Treats the decision rule as the independent variable, as the paper does when it separates who argues from who decides; the finding that extra rounds before the decision lower accuracy matches 16.10 and 16.16, where the exchange edges and narration amplify objection without improving the verdict, and its protocol comparison is the reference point for the paper's choice of an uninterested moderator over a seat majority.

verified_entries.title: When and Why Does Multi-Agent Debate Fail and Does It Really Underperform?
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Analyses the incentive structure of competitive debate (agents hold opposing positions) and consensus-seeking debate and finds both suffer debate hacking: competitive debate reduces to a cheap-talk game in which agents send misleading messages to win, while consensus-seeking debate suppresses informative disagreement; proposes ColMAD, a non-zero-sum collaborative protocol that beats prior protocols by up to 10 points and single-agent baselines at matched budget (abstract). arXiv v2 (14 July 2026), comments 'Preprint, ongoing work'.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Names the same theory the paper's design comes from, cheap talk among opposed advocates, and reaches the opposite prescription: they abandon opposed positions because advocates mislead to win, whereas the paper keeps the opposition and reads the against-interest objection as the credible signal (claim 3), so the paper answers their debate-hacking objection by showing what a locked advocate's rare deviation is worth rather than by removing the stake.

verified_entries.title: Wisdom of LLM Crowds: Aggregation and Contamination in Language Model Ensembles
verified_entries.what_it_shows: Elicits probability estimates from 15 LLMs on 254 binary prediction-market questions; learned aggregators (logistic regression and an MLP) beat every individual model and every classical aggregation rule, the linear rule matches the network, symbolic regression recovers a pure model-disagreement signal as the simplest useful formula, and training-cutoff contamination collapses the apparent gap between frontier and small models from 35.8 to 8.9 percent on clean questions (abstract). arXiv v2 (22 July 2026) used; search results report an ACM Transactions on Social Computing version at DOI 10.1145/3839337, which resolves to dl.acm.org but the landing page returned 403, so that venue is unverified.
verified_entries.relation_to_paper: Positions claim (2)'s next step and claim (3)'s principle: a cross-vendor panel gains over its best member only under a learned weighted rule, not a simple majority, which is the decider 16.18's third branch says to test next, and its recovery of model disagreement as the useful signal is the ensemble analogue of the paper's flag, where a second objecting seat, not the vote, carries the information.
